heading: Hook and context · 0:00–0:38
text: Ever wondered why a piece of bread starts to taste sweet if you keep it in your mouth long enough? Something in your saliva is cutting starch into sugar, right there, while the cells of your tongue sit in the same liquid untouched. That something is an enzyme. Your body runs thousands of reactions at once, at body temperature, and left to themselves many would be far too slow to keep you alive. Enzymes speed particular reactions by acting on suitable substrates. How, and where, is this lesson.

heading: What you will be able to do · 0:38–1:05
text: By the end you will be able to state what an enzyme is and where it works, inside a cell or outside it; explain how an enzyme works, using the active site, the enzyme–substrate complex, the lowering of activation energy and specificity; and keep the two hypotheses, lock-and-key and induced fit, as two separate pictures with two separate names.

heading: A globular protein, and a catalyst · 1:05–1:50
text: Start with what an enzyme is. An enzyme is a globular protein: one or more polypeptide chains folded into a compact shape, the kind you met in the protein lessons. Its job is to be a biological catalyst: it increases the rate of a reaction, and when the reaction is complete the enzyme itself is unchanged, ready to go again. Its folded structure forms the active site we will look at next.

heading: Inside the cell, or secreted to work outside · 1:50–2:38
text: Now, where does it work? Some enzymes catalyse reactions inside the cell that made them. Catalase is one: it breaks down hydrogen peroxide inside cells. We call those intracellular enzymes. Others are made in a cell and then secreted, released out of the cell, to catalyse reactions outside it. The amylase in your saliva is one, released into your mouth to work on starch out there; lipase in your intestine is another. Those are extracellular enzymes. Same kind of molecule; the difference is where the reaction happens.

heading: COMMON MISTAKE E32: the wrong prefix · 2:38–3:35
text: Here is a mistake the examiners list for exactly this word, on the card. The question asked for the term that describes an enzyme which is secreted and catalyses reactions outside cells. Read this answer. Look at the prefix. It starts with ex, it ends with cellular, and it feels right, because ex means out and the enzyme is out of the cell. One reason this can feel right is that they have just learnt that the enzyme leaves the cell, and the word for leaving blurs into the word for where it works. But the examiners' list of common mistakes shows four different ex words offered, and the term credited is extracellular: the syllabus's own word, and the one credited in November 2020 when you had to underline the terms that describe lipases. So write it in full, extracellular enzyme. And catalyst on its own was not credited either: it says what the enzyme does, not where.

heading: The fold, and the active site · 3:35–4:12
text: Look closely at the enzyme, because the whole explanation is about shape. This model shows one folded polypeptide. Its tertiary structure is held by interactions between R groups, from the protein lessons. On that folded surface is a small region, a cleft or pocket, with a very particular shape: the active site. Its shape is set by the whole fold around it, and the catalysis happens here.

heading: Specificity: complementary, not the same shape · 4:12–4:58
text: Now watch three different molecules try the active site. This one drifts in and does not fit; it slides off. This one, the same. This one settles in, cleanly. The active site is complementary in shape to this substrate: not the same shape, complementary. That is enzyme specificity: an enzyme acts on a particular substrate or a limited group of related substrates. These two molecules do not fit this active site. Picture a lock and a key; and written properly: the active site is complementary in shape to its substrate, so the enzyme is specific.

heading: Held in place: the enzyme–substrate complex · 4:58–5:32
text: When the substrate seats, it is held in place by temporary bonds between the substrate and the R groups lining the active site: hydrogen bonds, for example. Enzyme and substrate bound together like this is the enzyme–substrate complex, and you write that name out in full. This is the moment the lesson has been building to, because it is inside this complex that the reaction actually happens.

heading: Inside the complex: the reaction, and the enzyme goes again · 5:32–6:40
text: Take a real reaction so you can see it. Amylase is our enzyme and a stretch of starch is its substrate: four glucose units in a chain, atom by atom in the inset. Inside the complex a molecule of water is used and one glycosidic bond is broken, the net change from the carbohydrate lessons. The bridge oxygen keeps its bond to carbon one and takes a hydrogen from the water; the water's remaining O–H goes to carbon four on the other side. One chain of four becomes two molecules of maltose: the products, and they leave the active site. Now look at the enzyme: nothing about it has changed. Same fold, same active site. That is what catalyst meant.

heading: Why it is faster: activation energy · 6:40–7:40
text: Why is it faster? Here is an energy profile for this reaction: energy up the side, the progress of the reaction along the bottom. The substrate starts here; the product ends here, in this example a little lower; and in between there is a hill. To react, the substrate has to get over that hill, and its height is the activation energy, the energy that has to be put in before the reaction can go. The enzyme lowers the activation energy: same start, same finish, a lower hill. The gap between the two peaks is the reduction, not either hill on its own. A lower hill means many more molecules get over it in a given time, so the rate goes up.

heading: COMMON MISTAKE E35: the sentence that answers every question except this one · 7:40–8:45
text: Here is a mistake that comes from knowing this lesson well, on the card. In June 2016, Paper 22 asked why glycogen branching enzyme is needed in addition to glycogen synthase. Read this answer. Look at what this answer says about glycogen branching enzyme in particular. It mentions branches, but does not identify the bond. Lowering activation energy is true of enzymes generally; forming branches is this enzyme's role. Naming the particular bond is one way to make this answer precise. This can feel like a useful answer because it is the sentence they have just learnt, and it is not false. But the question was about this enzyme's precise job, and the examiners' comment says the common mistake was being too general rather than stating the type of bond this enzyme catalyses. Glycogen is branched because of alpha one-six glycosidic bonds, from the carbohydrate lessons, and those are what this enzyme makes. So the credited answer names the bond: it catalyses the formation of alpha one-six glycosidic bonds. Now the boundary: that is a ruling about that question. Where a question asks for the mode of action of an enzyme, lowering activation energy can be a marking point; June 2024 credited it for laccase. Keep the sentence; make sure it answers the question in front of you.

heading: The lock-and-key hypothesis · 8:45–9:25
text: Now the two hypotheses, and keep them as two separate drawings. The first and older one is the lock-and-key hypothesis. The active site has a fixed shape that is complementary to the substrate before the substrate arrives, like a lock cut for one key. The substrate fits, the complex forms, the products leave, and the active site has the same shape throughout. This is not a wrong picture: when June 2024 asked for diagrams of the lock-and-key hypothesis for lysozyme, those diagrams earned the marks. It is the simpler model, and it explains specificity.

heading: The induced-fit hypothesis · 9:25–10:10
text: The second is the induced-fit hypothesis. At rest, the active site is not fully complementary to the substrate. As the substrate binds, the active site changes shape to fit it, becoming fully complementary, and the complex forms. After the reaction the products leave, and the enzyme returns to its original shape. Watch the drawing: the resting shape, the change on binding, the return. Induced fit is the refinement now generally accepted, and the credited phrase is exactly that: the active site changes shape to fit the substrate. Two ideas, two names.

heading: COMMON MISTAKE E33: two names glued together · 10:10–11:05
text: And that brings us to a mistake the examiners list word for word, on the card. The question asked for the name of the hypothesis in which the active site changes shape as the substrate binds. Read this answer. Look at the words. There are two hypotheses in this lesson, and this answer has taken a piece of each and glued them together. The names can merge when both are taught together. But they are different pictures: lock-and-key is the fixed shape, induced fit is the shape that changes. The examiners' list shows five of these hybrids, and it says they were looking only for induced fit. So: two drawings, two names in your pen, lock-and-key or induced fit, never a blend of the two.

heading: The sentence you write · 11:05–11:35
text: Now build the sentence the examiners credit, clause by clause. The active site of the enzyme is complementary to its substrate. The substrate binds, forming an enzyme–substrate complex. The enzyme lowers the activation energy, so the reaction is faster. The products are released, and the enzyme is unchanged and used again.

heading: COMMON MISTAKE E34: the labels on the drawing · 11:50–13:05
text: Last mistake, and it is on the drawing itself, on the card. June 2024, Paper 22, asked for labelled diagrams showing how the lock-and-key hypothesis explains the action of lysozyme on peptidoglycan. Here is a drawing of the kind the report describes. Read it. Start with the labels. The big shape with the cleft is labelled peptidoglycan, and the small piece is labelled lysozyme. They are the wrong way round. Lysozyme is the enzyme, the protein with the active site; peptidoglycan is what it acts on, the substrate. An easy swap when both names are unfamiliar and arrive in one sentence. Next, look where the active site has been drawn: on the small piece. The active site is a region of the enzyme, so it belongs in the big shape's cleft. And the last one costs: the complex is labelled E S C. The report for that paper says enzyme-substrate complex, written out, should have been used. So: swap the two names; move the active site onto the enzyme; write the complex out in full. Now the drawing earns its marks.

heading: What I told you, read off the model · 13:05–13:50
text: So here is the whole lesson on the model you have been looking at. An enzyme is a globular protein and a biological catalyst; some work inside the cell, intracellular, and some are secreted to work outside, extracellular. On the enzyme, the active site, complementary to its substrate: that is specificity. The substrate binds, held by temporary bonds: the enzyme–substrate complex. Inside it the reaction happens with a lower activation energy, so it is faster. The products leave and the enzyme is unchanged. Two hypotheses: lock-and-key, a fixed shape; induced fit, the active site changes shape to fit and returns afterwards.

heading: How it is asked, with the real question on screen · 13:50–15:15
text: Now, how this reaches you in an exam. They ask you to draw labelled diagrams, and in June 2024 full marks needed a label or annotation linking the drawing to the supplied example. They ask you to describe and explain the mode of action of a named enzyme, and in the laccase question, full marks needed a reference to laccase or its substrates. For substrate binding, describe complementary shapes. Here is the drawing question. Read it, then watch the credited points land on our model. And the bread? Amylase, extracellular, in your saliva, with an active site complementary to starch; your tongue's cells are not its substrate.
